Magnesia Ancient City | Magnesia on the Maeander
On the banks of the Maeander, the city of white-browed Artemis

At the foot of Mount Gümüşdağ, overlooking the plain of the Great Maeander, Magnesia is one of Ionia’s hidden treasures — home to the Temple of Artemis Leukophryene designed by Hermogenes, one of the best-preserved stadiums in Anatolia, and a history spanning more than 2,400 years.

A story that stretches from Thessaly to the Maeander

According to legend, the city was founded by the Magnetes, who came from the region of Thessaly in Greece and gave the city its name. Magnesia on the Maeander (Latin Magnesia ad Maeandrum) therefore carries deep ties to the far shore of the Aegean.

Today the city lies near Ortaklar in the Germencik district of Aydın, within the boundaries of the village of Tekin. To the north rises Mount Gümüşdağ, known in antiquity as Thorax; through the city flows the Gümüşçay, called Lethaios in ancient times. Its proximity to the great Ionian cities of Ephesus, Priene and Miletus made Magnesia a crossroads of the region’s trade and pilgrimage routes.

At the heart of the city stood Artemis, worshipped under the epithet Leukophryene, meaning “white-browed”. The Leukophryena festival held in the goddess’s honour won international prestige through embassies sent to cities across the Greek world.
Though the temple at Magnesia is smaller than the one at Ephesus, it far surpasses it in harmony and in the skill with which the sanctuary is laid out.

Not to be confused: This page is about Magnesia on the Maeander in Aydın. Magnesia ad Sipylum (Magnesia under Mount Sipylus), the ancient name of Manisa, is a different city; the famous Battle of Magnesia in 190 BC was fought there.
Key milestones in Magnesia’s history — from its relocation away from its first site, through its Hellenistic brilliance, to the Byzantine era.

The Magnetes from Thessaly found the first city on the banks of the Maeander. In the 7th century BC the city is devastated by a Cimmerian attack, after which it comes under Lydian and then Persian rule.

Themistocles, the Athenian commander who won the Battle of Salamis, takes refuge with the Persian king after being exiled. The king grants him the revenues of Magnesia, and Themistocles spends the last years of his life here.
A new city, a new order
Under the Spartan commander Thibron, the city is moved next to the sanctuary of Leukophrys at the foot of Mount Thorax. The Magnesia we walk through today is this new city with its grid plan.
The sanctuary of Artemis gains international recognition. The architect Hermogenes transforms the face of the city with the temples of Artemis Leukophryene and Zeus Sosipolis.
The city remains prosperous in the Roman province of Asia. The stadium, theatre, odeon and bath-gymnasium complexes are enlarged, and the city is adorned with monumental buildings.
A bishopric in the Byzantine period, the city shrinks within a reduced circuit of walls. Over time, earthquakes and the silt carried by the Gümüşçay bury its buildings underground.
Following the work of Charles Texier in the 1840s and Carl Humann in the 1890s, the city is being brought back to life by excavations carried out by Ankara University teams since 1984.
What can you see in the city?
The buildings uncovered by excavation offer outstanding examples of Hellenistic town planning and the Roman culture of public spectacle.

Hermogenes’ Ionic pseudodipteral temple, with a platform of roughly 41 × 67 m, was one of the largest temples in Anatolia. Its frieze depicting the battle of the Amazons is now in some of the world’s leading museums.
Agora and Temple of Zeus Sosipolis
The vast agora, surrounded by stoas, was the city’s commercial and political centre. Within it rose the small but elegant Temple of Zeus Sosipolis, dedicated to Zeus “the saviour of the city”.
One of the best-preserved stadiums in Anatolia. With its rows of seats, honorary boxes and athletes’ entrances, it is thought to have held around 30,000 spectators.
The Hellenistic theatre, set against the slope of Mount Gümüşdağ, was enlarged in the Roman period. The odeon, which hosted council meetings and concerts, is a smaller and more elegant building.
The gymnasium, where young men received physical and intellectual training, was combined with baths in the Roman period and became one of the liveliest centres of the city’s social life.
Besides the walls that encircled the Hellenistic city, a reduced Byzantine defensive line and the remains of churches shed light on the city’s later life.
Hermogenes: the architect who rewrote the rules

One of the most influential architects of the Hellenistic age, Hermogenes inspired the Roman architect Vitruvius centuries later with the system of proportions he applied at Magnesia. Vitruvius praises him by name in his Ten Books on Architecture.
An innovative plan that removes the inner row of columns, preserving the grandeur of a double-colonnaded temple while leaving visitors a wide gallery.
An arrangement in which the spacing between columns is set by the column diameter, regarded as “ideal” for both strength and beauty.
A design approach based on a grid, in which the entire building is composed from a single unit of measurement — a turning point in Ionic architecture.

A selection of scholarly studies on Magnesia. The full texts can be read free of charge on the websites of the journals that published them; the summaries below are short introductions written for this page. Most of the articles are in Turkish.

Traces, in order, the travels, research and excavations carried out at the site since the first recorded visit in 1715. It brings together the city’s “story of discovery”, from the 19th-century work of Texier and Humann, through the long silence after 1893, to the renewed Turkish excavations led by Orhan Bingöl.
Orhan Bingöl, Görkem Kökdemir, Muharrem Oral · Anadolu/Anatolia 34 (2008)

Reports the results of three excavation seasons at the stadium. Besides the seating sections, galleries and podium, it presents the monumental entrance, the starting mechanism for races (hysplex), the podium reliefs and inscriptions.

Reconsiders why Hermogenes chose the pseudodipteral plan for the Temple of Artemis. According to the author, the purpose of the wide colonnaded gallery was not a play of light and shadow but to display rich decoration such as friezes, capitals and coffered ceilings.

Seeks to re-date the monumental gateway (Propylon) between the Sanctuary of Artemis and the agora on the basis of its decoration. Through a comparative study of anthemion, kymation and acanthus motifs, it dates most of the decoration to the 1st century BC – 1st century AD.

Presents the building identified as a market basilica, located southwest of the Sanctuary of Artemis between the agora and the odeion. Based on the architectural elements from its fully excavated eastern part, it proposes reconstructions of the building’s original form.

Re-examines the inscription found in the first excavations that tells the city’s foundation legend. Using the inscription, coin images and details of sculptures, it studies the migration of the Magnetes from Thessaly via Crete to Anatolia and the founding hero Leukippos.

Investigates whether Athena was worshipped at Magnesia, under which epithet, and whether a Panathenaic festival like the one in Athens was held in the city. It proposes a new identification for a female head found near the theatre and now in the Istanbul Archaeological Museums.
Mevlüt Eliüşük, Fatma Bağdatlı Çam · Cedrus 10 (2022), pp. 211–228

Studies a marble female head found in the south stoa of the Sanctuary of Artemis. It argues that the head was first carved for a veiled female statue and later reworked to fit another body, and dates the piece to the Early Imperial period on stylistic grounds.

The official publication of the first major excavations in the city and the standard reference work for research on Magnesia (in German). It contains plans, drawings and excavation results for the Temple of Artemis, the altar, the agora and other buildings.
Orhan Bingöl, Magnesia ad Maeandrum – Menderes Magnesiası, Ankara, 1998.
Orhan Bingöl, Beyaz Kaşlı Artemis’in Kenti – Menderes Magnesiası, Istanbul, 2007 (archaeological guide; an English edition is also available).
Easily reached from Kuşadası, Söke and Aydın, Magnesia can be combined with Ephesus and Priene on a one-day tour of ancient cities.
Tekin Mahallesi, Ortaklar, Germencik / Aydın, Türkiye. Reached via the Ortaklar–Söke road.
About 5 km from Ortaklar and about 20 km from Söke. The easiest way to get there is by car; the nearest airport is İzmir Adnan Menderes.
For current opening hours and admission fees, please check the official site page of the Turkish Ministry of Culture and Tourism.
Summer temperatures are very high, so go early in the morning or late in the afternoon. Bring comfortable shoes, a hat and water. In spring the site is transformed by wildflowers.
